top_strength: The pricing and clock block was clean, complete and confident. Garrison led with the simple-pricing frame, gave the rate, listed what's inside it, and then proactively flagged the two things that sit outside it rather than burying them - packing supplies and the Round Rock trip fee: "It is a little bit outside of our free working zone. So we do have a trip fee of $75 per truck that we send out that way." He ran the full clock explanation (on-site start, two-and-a-half hour minimum, fifteen-minute increments) and closed it with a real sense-check, "Does that all make sense so far." He also checked date availability before anything else and caught the mother-in-law drop-off as a second stop, probing its address, floor and bedroom count without being asked.
coaching_note: The estimate fell apart at the exact moment it mattered. Garrison told a 3,500 sq ft customer "seven to nine movers for seven to nine hours" - that crew size is wrong and it is the number she will carry into her comparison shopping. Worse, he built it "assuming no packing" after she had just told him "that's the thing that I'm most stressed about is the packing portion of it" and asked about full-service packing twice. Before quoting, confirm out loud whether packing is in or out, then give one coherent crew-and-hours number with a dollar range attached. The virtual walkthrough is the right instinct for this home, but she declined it, so the number he gave on the phone became the real quote - it has to be defensible on its own.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and affirming but heavily padded with filler ("absolutely, absolutely," "very, very, very very general"), he never used the customer's name once, and he let her explicit stress cue about packing pass without acknowledgment.
